criteria.descriptor: Full marks: mechanisms are correct and used precisely — strangler-fig extraction behind a stable interface, idempotent backfill from a snapshot offset, event-log-driven catch-up with idempotent consumers and a high-water mark, shadow traffic + offline recall/nDCG eval, canary with guardrails, and flag-based instant rollback. Correctly identifies why app dual-writes are riskier than a replayable log, why embedding-model parity matters, and why deletions/tombstones must propagate. Deduct for technically wrong claims (e.g. treating the vector store as static, claiming dual-writes are consistent by default, or asserting latency health alone proves no quality regression).

Full marks: covers all four required areas — migration pattern/topology, consistency under continuous ingestion (backfill + catch-up + reconciliation), pre-serving validation (shadow + offline eval), and detection + instant rollback — and notes the parallel-run cost and a decommission/bake step. Deduct for each missing area, especially omitting the continuous-ingestion catch-up or the rollback/fallback design.

Full marks: justifies the key choices — why incremental over big-bang, why an event log over dual-writes, why canary over blue-green for a quality-sensitive change, why the old store stays hot until a bake period completes, and why the embedding model is held constant. Weaker answers assert steps without explaining the trade-offs or the failure modes they prevent.

Full marks: organised into clear phases with a legible topology, correct vocabulary (facade/gateway, backfill, high-water mark, shadow/canary, guardrail, tombstone), and an unambiguous end-to-end sequence a reviewer could act on. Deduct for disorganised, vague, or jargon-dropping prose that never forms a coherent plan.

expected_answer_points: Uses an incremental strangler-fig approach with a stable retrieval interface/facade so both store implementations run behind one call site, and sequences the two changes (service extraction vs store swap) to change one variable at a time rather than a big-bang cutover

Handles never-stopping ingestion with a bulk idempotent backfill (upsert by doc id from a known offset) plus a catch-up mechanism, preferring a single durable ordered event log with idempotent per-store consumers over app-level dual-writes, and tracks a high-water mark
Includes reconciliation/drift detection (counts, checksums, sampled NN comparison) and correct deletion/tombstone propagation to both stores

Validates quality before serving via shadow/mirror traffic and an offline eval harness (recall@k / overlap / nDCG on a golden set) plus downstream answer-quality eval, keeping the embedding model/version constant to isolate the variable
Progressive canary cutover (1%->5%->25%->100%) via feature flag/router with online guardrails, and contrasts it against blue-green with the trade-off stated

Defines explicit guardrail metrics with thresholds (recall proxy, p99 latency, error rate, downstream quality/user feedback) and wires instant automated rollback as a routing/flag change, not a redeploy or re-migration

Keeps the old store hot and dual-fed through a bake period as the fallback and decommissions only after sustained confidence, while acknowledging the cost/operational overhead of running two stores in parallel
common_pitfalls: Proposes a big-bang cutover — freeze ingestion, dump-and-load, flip DNS — treating a continuously-mutated store as a static one-time copy, with no shadow validation and no instant rollback
Does only a one-time backfill and assumes the two stores stay consistent, missing the catch-up/replay mechanism, high-water-mark parity check, and reconciliation needed to prevent drift
Relies on naive application-level dual-writes without acknowledging partial-failure and ordering hazards, instead of a replayable event log with idempotent consumers
Validates only that the new service responds with low latency and no errors, conflating 'healthy' with 'no quality regression', so a silent recall/nDCG drop ships to users
Swaps the embedding model at the same time as the store, confounding the comparison so any regression cannot be attributed to the migration
Rollback plan requires a redeploy or re-migration rather than a flag/traffic flip, and/or decommissions the FAISS store before a bake period, leaving no consistent fallback to roll back to
reference_answer:
Pattern & topology (strangler fig, one variable at a time). First reduce blast radius by decoupling the two changes. Introduce a stable retrieval interface (a facade/gateway) at the monolith's call site so callers don't know the backend. Extract retrieval behind that interface as its own service while it still talks to FAISS — this proves the service boundary with no data risk. Then make the store pluggable behind the same interface, with old (FAISS) and new (managed cluster) implementations selectable per-request via a feature flag/router. This lets both run in parallel and makes cutover and rollback a routing decision, not a redeploy.

Data consistency under continuous ingestion. A one-time dump-and-load is wrong because ingestion never stops. Do a bulk backfill first: export the 200M embeddings and idempotent-upsert them into the new store keyed by document id, snapshotting at a known log offset/timestamp. Then catch up the tail. Prefer feeding both stores from a single durable, ordered event stream (Kafka/CDC) with idempotent consumers per store, rather than app-level dual-writes — dual-writes fail partially and lose ordering, whereas a replayable log lets a lagging store catch up and be re-driven after any fault. Track a high-water mark per store to confirm the new one has reached parity, and run periodic reconciliation (counts, checksums, sampled nearest-neighbour comparison, tombstone/deletion propagation) to catch drift. Keep the embedding model/version identical across stores so you're changing one variable; re-embedding is a separate migration.

Validation before serving. Shadow (mirror) live queries to both backends: serve from FAISS, log the new store's results, and compare offline — recall@k / result overlap, nDCG on a labelled golden query set, and p50/p99 latency — plus downstream answer quality (LLM-judge or human eval). This surfaces silent recall regressions with zero user impact.

Progressive cutover. Once shadow metrics are green, canary real traffic through the flag: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%, watching online guardrails at each step. Blue-green gives an instant flip but bets everything at once; canary is safer for a quality-sensitive change, so I default to canary.

Detect & roll back. Define guardrail thresholds — recall proxy (overlap vs old), p99 latency, error rate, and a downstream quality signal (answer eval / thumbs-down rate) — and wire automated rollback: on breach, the flag routes 100% back to FAISS instantly. Crucially, keep the old store hot and dual-fed from the event stream through a bake period so there is always a consistent fallback; decommission FAISS (and the monolith coupling) only after sustained confidence. Call out the costs made explicit by this plan: running two stores in parallel, index-build resource contention, and metadata/dimension parity.
